This game is set in 1975 and runs into the 90s; the punch-drunk old man is not edgy flavor, he is the central moral fact of managing fighters in that era, and the player must be allowed to look away and be remembered for it by the ledger. If it only ever happens to world fighters and never to YOUR man, the game is lying.

The joyful events (washing machine, watercolors, cigars, the watch) must fire with NO choices attached and no optimization angle — some of them barely move a number. The design temptation will be to bolt decisions and rewards onto them. Resist it. Gyms run on the mornings somebody's mother got a washing machine; those moments land precisely because the player can't play them, only witness them. That's what keeps a 15-year save from curdling into a spreadsheet.

role: Retired Promoter — thirty years of club shows, casino floors, and network lunches. My beat: where the money comes from, what it costs to take it, and how the business under the player's feet changes from 1975 to the 1990s.

scriptedEvents.title: The King Who Can't Say No
scriptedEvents.window: 1975-1978 (arc seeded at save creation; retirement date varies ±18 months)
scriptedEvents.analogOf: The late-Ali era: an aging, beloved heavyweight champion whose name alone floats the whole division's economy — and whose departure craters it.
beats: 1975: the paper carries the fading heavyweight king constantly — a poet in press conferences, slower every fight. Heavyweight purses run hot at every level; even club heavyweights get called.
Year 2 of the arc: he wins one he should have lost. Column inches double. A national closed-circuit superfight fires (see world effects).
Year 3: he loses the title in an upset the writers call a funeral. Wins it back or doesn't — seeded per save.
Arc end: retirement announcement, one page of the paper is nothing else for two weeks. Then the division goes quiet: heavyweight offers thin out for years, until the young-destroyer event.
worldEffects: While active: heavyweight purse multiplier ×1.6 at all levels (pursefor gets an era term); heavyweight walk-in frequency +25% (every kid wants to be him)
One 'superfight week' per year of the arc: all offers that week pay ×1.25, venues report sellouts in press clippings
On retirement: heavyweight purse multiplier decays to ×0.75 over 12 months and stays there until the young-destroyer event fires; heavyweight offer frequency −30%
The national #1 heavyweight slot in the world population churns twice in three years (short reigns, no draw)
scriptedEvents.playerFacing: Clippings track the whole arc. If the player has a heavyweight with publicReputation ≥ 25 during the boom, a promoter phone call offers an undercard slot on a closed-circuit show at ×2 purse. On retirement day, the gym log: 'Nobody hit the bags much today. The radio was on.'

scriptedEvents.title: The Networks Come Calling
scriptedEvents.window: 1976-1978 (seeded per save)
scriptedEvents.analogOf: The late-70s network boxing boom — weekend-afternoon fights on free TV, hungry for telegenic prospects with clean records.
beats: A clipping: a national network announces a weekly fight card, 'bringing boxing back to the American living room.'
Over 6 months, TV dates appear in the offer pool: 6- and 8-rounders paying ×2.5 club scale, flagged 'television' in the pitch.
TV matchmakers develop a visible taste: unbeaten records, KO percentage, a face. The paper starts printing records in headlines where it didn't before.
The boom holds until the tournament-scandal event kills it.
worldEffects: New offer type: TV date — purse ×2.5, but eligibility gated on record (losses ≤ 1 OR wins ≥ 12 with kos/wins ≥ 0.5) and publicReputation ≥ 20
Winning on TV: publicReputation +6 to +10 instead of the normal swing; losing on TV: −6 and no TV offers for that fighter for 18 months
World-sim rival prospects with clean records rise in publicReputation faster during the era (the whole scene starts protecting records)
scriptedEvents.playerFacing: Phone call in the office, a new voice: 'I do the matchmaking for the network date. I'm looking at your boy's record. Keep it clean and we'll talk.' The condition is stated, never enforced by rule — the player learns the business teaches you to duck.

scriptedEvents.title: The Tournament With the Crooked Ledger
scriptedEvents.window: 1979-1982 (fires 2-4 years after network-fight-nights)
scriptedEvents.analogOf: The 1977 U.S. Championships scandal — a nationally televised tournament collapsing when fighter records and ratings were found to be fabricated, souring network TV on the sport.
beats: A famous promoter announces a televised national tournament to crown 'people's champions' in five divisions. Entry invitations go out — including, possibly, to the player (see below).
Two rounds in, a wire-service story: records of several entrants were invented, ratings bought. Named quietly: the ratings man took envelopes.
The network pulls the plug mid-tournament. Hearings in the paper for a month. Nobody goes to jail.
Network money exits: TV dates vanish from the offer pool within 60 days and stay gone until cable-money.
worldEffects: If a player fighter was entered: purse for completed rounds paid, tournament ranking voided, publicReputation −4 (tainted by association) unless he won every bout by KO (the paper calls him 'the one honest thing in it,' +6)
TV-date offer type removed from the pool for 2-3 years
All purses −15% for 12 months (the sport's whole price structure sags when TV leaves)
One fictional promoter NPC is permanently marked 'crooked' in the press; his later offers (he keeps promoting — they always do) pay ×1.2 but carry a 20% chance of the bounced-check event
scriptedEvents.playerFacing: If any player fighter has wins ≥ 8 and losses ≤ 2 when it fires: a fat envelope arrives — tournament invitation, guaranteed three purses at ×3 scale. Taking it is free money with a delayed cost. The collapse plays out in clippings either way.

scriptedEvents.title: The Desert Buys the Sport
scriptedEvents.window: 1977-1980 (seeded per save)
scriptedEvents.analogOf: The casino era — Las Vegas consolidating big-fight economics and Atlantic City legalizing in 1976-78, turning casinos into the sport's paymasters.
beats: Clippings: a second gambling town legalizes casinos back East. Then: a desert casino pays an unheard-of site fee for a title fight.
Casino venues enter the offer pool — 'the Sands of the game's fiction,' fictional names, flagged in the venue line.
Casino cards want two things: names for the marquee and reliable losers for the names. The B-side economy is born.
By arc end, every fight above 8 rounds that matters happens in a casino ballroom. The club circuit starts its long death (club-show-collapse).
worldEffects: New venue class: casino — all purses at casino venues ×2 to ×3
Casino offers skew hard: for player fighters with publicReputation < 40 they are almost always 'reach' risk (you're the opponent); above 55, almost always 'soft' (you're the attraction)
Vegas — present but locked in the city list — begins appearing as a venue on the biggest offers, a place your men go to fight but you can't yet live
Site-fee economics: title and 10-round main events gain a flat era bonus (+$2,000 base-1975, inflated)
scriptedEvents.playerFacing: The first casino offer is a phone call with a new texture: 'The purse is three times your last one. I'll be honest with you, friend — my guy needs a win and your guy has a pulse and a record. That's the job.' The pitch says out loud what club promoters only implied.

scriptedEvents.title: The Armory Goes Dark
scriptedEvents.window: 1978-1984 (rolling; one venue every 12-24 months)
scriptedEvents.analogOf: The death of the American club-show circuit — neighborhood fight venues closing through the late 70s and 80s as TV and casinos absorbed the sport.
beats: One of the player city's persistent press venues (press.ts venues array) announces its last card. A clipping mourns it in two paragraphs.
Offer frequency for 4- and 6-rounders in the home city drops a step each closure.
A generation problem surfaces in the paper: 'Where does a kid get ten fights now?' Rival gyms' prospects visibly stall at 3-1, 4-2 records in the world sim.
What replaces it, in order: casino undercards (travel), TV dates (gatekept), and — late 80s — a cable network's small-hall series that quietly revives short cards at ×1.3 old club scale.
worldEffects: Each closure: remove one venue from press venues, −20% frequency on 4/6-round offers in home city (cumulative)
Green fighters (record < 5 fights) take longer to get offers — MIN_TENURE stays but offer chance for novices halves by 1984
Casino/TV offers include travel: −$60 base-1975 (inflated) expense line against any purse at an out-of-city venue
Late beat (1986-89): 'small-hall series' restores novice offer frequency to ~80% of 1975 levels
scriptedEvents.playerFacing: The closure is a clipping plus a gym-log line: 'Somebody taped the Armory's last fight bill inside the locker room door.' The squeeze is felt, not announced — the phone just rings less for your green kids, and the player who reads the paper knows why.

scriptedEvents.title: Nobody's Buying Tickets
scriptedEvents.analogOf: The 1980-82 recession (and the early-90s dip) hitting gate-driven small boxing hardest while inflation kept running.
beats: Clippings turn economic: layoffs at the plant, a promoter quoted saying 'the ten-dollar seat is dead here.'
Purse offers stop keeping pace with inflation for ~24 months — the numbers look the same as last year, which means they're smaller.
Gate-percentage deals vanish; flat purses only. A couple of world-sim rival gyms fold outright (rosters scatter, a few fighters go independent).
Recovery is quiet: one spring the offers are just better again.
worldEffects: Purse inflation term frozen for the window (pursefor uses inflationFactor(windowStart) while active) — a real ~12% pay cut by the end
Offer frequency −25%; 'reach' offers become relatively more common (desperate matchmakers pay for danger, not names)
1-2 rival gyms in the region fold; their best men hit the independent pool (a poaching opportunity, if the player's gym has room and reputation)
Fighter dues: broke-fighter rate rises from 15% to 25% among walk-ins during the window
scriptedEvents.playerFacing: Felt in the ledger before it's read in the paper. One phone call makes it explicit: a promoter offering last year's number, and when pressed — 'That's the purse. Take it or I'll find somebody hungrier. There's a lot of hungry right now.'

scriptedEvents.title: The Four Names Everyone Knows
scriptedEvents.window: 1980-1987 (four fictional stars seeded at save creation in the 147-160 divisions)
scriptedEvents.analogOf: The Four Kings era — Leonard/Hearns/Hagler/Durán making the welterweight and middleweight divisions the sport's economic center for a decade.
beats: Four world-sim fighters — a smiling Olympic darling, a skeletal puncher, a shaven-skulled grinder nobody promotes willingly, and an aging brawler with fists like history — rise through the rankings clippings across 1978-80.
They fight each other in a round-robin of superfights over the window, each one a closed-circuit (later PPV) event the paper covers for a month.
The whole 140-160 band becomes the money band: everything near their divisions pays more, and every card wants welter/middle bouts.
By 1987 they've all fought each other twice; two retire, one won't. The band cools to normal.
worldEffects: Welterweight/middleweight purse multiplier ×1.5 for the window; light-heavy/heavyweight unaffected (the point: the money moved DOWN the scale for once)
Undercard slots on the four superfight cards enter the offer pool for player fighters at 140-160 with publicReputation ≥ 30: purse ×3, B-side risk profile
A player fighter who beats any opponent 'out of' one of the four stars' camps gets double the reputation swing
Welterweight/middleweight walk-in frequency +20% during the window
scriptedEvents.playerFacing: The four names saturate the clippings for years — the game's proof the world has its own greats. If the player has the right fighter, the superfight-undercard call is the era's signature offer: the most money he's ever been offered, to be furniture on someone else's night.

scriptedEvents.title: The Night the Sport Went Quiet
scriptedEvents.window: 1981-1984 (seeded per save; involves world-sim fighters only, never the player's bout)
scriptedEvents.analogOf: The Duk Koo Kim tragedy (1982) and its aftermath: title fights cut from 15 to 12 rounds, mandatory medicals, standing-eight and suspension rules, an insurance squeeze on small promoters.
beats: A nationally televised lightweight title fight ends with one man in a coma. He dies four days later. The paper's tone changes completely for a month — editorials asking whether the sport should exist.
A congressman holds hearings (clippings, two beats). The sanctioning councils cut championship distance from 15 rounds to 12, loudly.
State commissions add mandatory pre-fight medicals and post-KO suspensions. Insurance for promoters triples; several small operators quit rather than pay.
A year on, the reforms are just how things are. The dead man's name resurfaces once a year in an anniversary column.
worldEffects: Permanent: title/10-round bouts capped at 12 rounds (engine scheduledRounds)
Permanent: post-KO-loss mandatory suspension — restUntil after a KO loss gets +30 days by commission rule, surfaced as a typed suspension notice
New per-bout cost: medical/licensing fee, $35 base-1975 (inflated) deducted from every purse from reform onward — itemized on the purse sheet
12-month chill: offer frequency −15%, KO-heavy 'reach' matchups rarer (matchmakers frightened of headlines)
scriptedEvents.playerFacing: Clippings carry the tragedy and hearings. The player's first post-reform purse arrives with a new deduction line typed on it: 'COMM. MEDICAL & LIC. — $35.' The gym log the week it happens: 'Sparring was careful today. Nobody said why.'

scriptedEvents.title: The Cable Wire Reaches the Gym
scriptedEvents.window: 1982-1985 (fires 1-3 years after tournament-scandal kills network TV)
scriptedEvents.analogOf: HBO/ESPN-era cable boxing — subscription and basic-cable networks becoming the sport's new paymasters after the networks left.
beats: A clipping: a 'pay-cable outfit' buys the rights to a title fight, and nobody's living room antenna can get it.
Two tiers form in the offer pool: a prestige cable network (big fights, big checks, wants names) and a basic-cable weeknight series (honest 8-10 rounders, wants action, forgives a loss).
The weeknight series becomes the working fighter's best friend — the first TV money since the scandal that doesn't demand an unbeaten record.
By arc end, 'What did the cable people say?' is the first question about any fight that matters.
worldEffects: TV dates return in two flavors: prestige (purse ×3.5, needs publicReputation ≥ 50) and weeknight series (purse ×1.8, needs record ≥ 10 fights and an 'action' profile — kos/wins ≥ 0.4 OR both men's styles aggressive)
Weeknight series is loss-tolerant: losing a good fight on it costs −3 reputation instead of TV-boom rules, and a great losing effort (competitive on cards, lionheart surfacing) can gain +2
Cable era makes fighter STYLE an economic fact for the first time — the offer pitch starts mentioning it
scriptedEvents.playerFacing: A young cable matchmaker phone call, different species from the network man: 'I don't care about the zero, I care about the fight. Your guy comes forward. My audience likes guys who come forward.' A door reopening for honest records — and for hot_tempered brawlers who were unsellable before.

scriptedEvents.title: The Kid Who Ended the Quiet
scriptedEvents.window: 1985-1988 (fires only after fading-king-farewell's doldrums have run ≥ 5 years)
scriptedEvents.analogOf: The Tyson phenomenon — a teenage heavyweight whose knockouts single-handedly reprice the heaviest division and drag the whole sport's casual audience back.
beats: A prospect notice from another city: a teenage heavyweight, 8-0 with 8 knockouts, none past the second round. The clippings come faster than for anyone before.
He wins a title before 21. Casino site fees for heavyweight cards triple in a season; his fights sell out in hours and end in minutes.
Everything heavyweight-adjacent inflates: sparring partners get paydays, undercard heavies get TV time, and any big kid who walks into a gym gets whispered about.
Seeded per save: he either reigns 4-6 years or loses in a historic upset to a 20-to-1 nobody — the biggest single clipping the game ever prints.
worldEffects: Heavyweight purse multiplier restored to ×2 (from the post-king ×0.75); heavyweight walk-in frequency +40% for the window

New offer type: sparring-partner contract — a player heavyweight with chin ≥ 55 and record ≥ 6 fights gets offered 4-week camp work at $1,500 base-1975 (inflated), no bout, small stamina/defense gain, 10% chance of returning with morale −8 ('he doesn't talk about camp')
Undercard offers on his cards: ×2.5 purse, huge exposure — win on one and publicReputation +12
If the upset fires: one week of purse chaos (all heavyweight offers ±40%), then the multiplier halves
scriptedEvents.playerFacing: Pure clippings until it touches the player: the sparring-camp telegram, or the undercard call. Gym log during the boom: 'Three big kids came in this week. Every one of them threw the right hand first.'

scriptedEvents.title: More Belts Than Bodies
scriptedEvents.window: 1983-1990 (two beats: a third council ~1983-85, a fourth ~1988-90)
scriptedEvents.analogOf: The sanctioning-body proliferation — IBF (1983) and WBO (1988) joining the WBA/WBC split, multiplying 'world champions,' rankings, and sanctioning fees.
beats: A clipping: a breakaway group of commissioners forms a new 'International Federation,' promising cleaner ratings. It publishes its own top-10 lists immediately.
Within a year it has champions. The paper prints division tables with two, then three names per weight class and an editorial: 'Who is the champion of anything?'
Five years later it happens again — a fourth body, run out of a hotel in another country. By 1990 a good fighter can be ranked by four organizations that all invoice him.
Permanent condition: title shots are easier to get and worth less, and every ranking costs money to keep.
worldEffects: National rankings duplicate per body: a player fighter can hold 1-4 separate rankings, each opening the ratings-assessment triggered event independently
Title-shot availability up (more belts), but title purse premium down ×0.6 per additional body's title vs the unified era
Press prints rankings tables from multiple bodies; a fighter dropped by one body for unpaid fees keeps the others (the shakedown has an escape valve, priced)
Unifying two belts becomes the rare prestige event: double reputation swing, stadium-show eligibility
scriptedEvents.playerFacing: Clippings, then invoices. The first letter from the new body is the tell: congratulations on your fighter's #9 ranking, and a 'ratings administration fee' schedule attached. The player learns the era's real product: the ranking is the thing they sell.

scriptedEvents.title: The Theater Comes Home
scriptedEvents.window: 1989-1993 (seeded per save)
scriptedEvents.analogOf: The closed-circuit-to-pay-per-view transition — big-fight revenue moving from theater seats to home cable boxes, and percentage deals becoming the top of the sport's economy.
beats: A clipping: a superfight grosses more from 'home pay-per-view' than from the arena and the theaters combined. The number printed is bigger than any purse the player has ever seen.
Closed-circuit theater offers (the desert-money era's percentage plays) disappear from the pool within two years.
PPV percentage offers replace them at the top: only for main events with a champion or top-3 name, but the upside is unbounded in a way flat purses never were.
The sport's split-personality is complete: PPV events and casino cards at the top, the small-hall cable series at the bottom, and almost nothing in between — the middle class of boxing is gone.
worldEffects: New offer structure for title/top-3 main events: flat purse OR (smaller guarantee + percentage of PPV buys, resolved against opponent reputation + combined publicReputation + a hype roll)
Percentage outcomes range ×0.5 to ×4 of the flat offer — the game's biggest single-night variance
Mid-tier 10-round non-TV offers thin out permanently (−30%) — the 'in between' fights stop paying
The player's ledger gains its first five-figure (inflated) single entries here if they have a champion
scriptedEvents.playerFacing: The percentage offer is a contract on the desk with two columns typed side by side: GUARANTEE and UPSIDE, and a promoter on the phone saying 'I'm offering you a piece of the future, friend. The flat number is for people who don't believe in their guy.'

triggeredEvents.title: Triple Money to Be the Opponent
triggeredEvents.trigger: desert-money era active + fighter hasLocker + record ≥ 6 fights + publicReputation 15-45 + not booked + restUntil passed
triggeredEvents.story: A casino matchmaker calls with three times your last purse. He's polite about it, which is how you know: your kid is the B-side. Their unbeaten house fighter needs a live body with a record, and yours reads right in the program.
choices: Take the money (book as 'reach' risk bout at ×3 purse)
Counter: ask for a rematch clause (purse drops to ×2.4, but if your man wins, a guaranteed follow-up offer at ×3 fires within 90 days)
Pass
effects: Take: purse = normal offer ×3; opponent drawn from window [mine×1.15, mine×1.45]; win = publicReputation +14 and a front-page clipping; KO loss = normal loss effects + no casino offers for that fighter for 12 months
Counter: 25% chance they hang up (offer lost, small chance of a 'difficult to deal with' note that shaves future casino offers for 6 months); otherwise as written
Pass: nothing — but the gym log notes the fighter heard about the number. If glory_hunter or chip_on_shoulder: morale −6
triggeredEvents.frequency: uncommon, repeatable (once per fighter per 18 months)

triggeredEvents.title: The Network Likes the Zero
triggeredEvents.trigger: network-fight-nights or cable-money (prestige tier) active + fighter losses = 0 + wins ≥ 6 + publicReputation ≥ 20
triggeredEvents.story: The television matchmaker wants your unbeaten kid for a date two months out — against an opponent of your choosing, he says, so long as the record stays pretty. He doesn't say 'stiff.' He says 'suitable.'
choices: Feed him a suitable opponent (auto-generates a 'soft' bout at TV purse ×2.5)
Match him honest (player picks a 'fair' offer from the pool at the same TV purse)
Turn the date down
effects: Suitable: near-certain win, purse ×2.5, publicReputation +5 — but a beat writer keeps a private 'protected' tally; at 3 protected TV wins, a column runs ('Who Has He Fought?'), publicReputation −8 and future reputation gains ×0.8 until he beats a 'fair' or 'reach' opponent
Honest: fair bout at ×2.5; a win pays publicReputation +9 and the writer's respect (one-time +3, clears any protected tally)
Decline: no cost; if the fighter is glory_hunter, morale +4 (he'd rather earn it) — if comfort_seeker, morale −4

triggeredEvents.title: The Man Wants to Buy Your Man
triggeredEvents.trigger: fighter publicReputation ≥ 55 OR nationally ranked + gym reputation below 'established' tier (the big fish circles small ponds)
triggeredEvents.story: A promoter you know by reputation — everyone does — invites you to lunch you didn't ask for. He wants your contender outright: a check for you, a signing bonus for the kid, and his machine behind the career. 'You've done fine work,' he says, the way a man compliments a house he's about to buy.
choices: Sell (fighter leaves roster)
Refuse politely
Refuse and let the paper know he came sniffing
effects: Sell: cash = $4,000 base-1975 × (publicReputation/50), inflated — the biggest single check available before a champion; fighter leaves, continues in world-sim under the promoter's banner (his clippings keep coming, a permanent might-have-been); every roster fighter with trust < 50 loses 8 more (they saw you sell a man); gym log goes quiet for a week
Refuse: fighter trust +10 if he learns of it (60% chance he does); the promoter's venues (2 casino names) stop offering that fighter dates for 24 months — the freeze-out is real and typed nowhere
Refuse loudly: fighter trust +12, gym reputation +small, clipping runs — but the promoter's freeze-out extends to your whole roster for 12 months

triggeredEvents.title: The Shot Comes With Strings
triggeredEvents.trigger: fighter nationally ranked top-10 + a champion in his division controlled by a promoter NPC (world-sim affiliation)
triggeredEvents.story: The title shot is available. The contract is eleven pages, and page nine is the one that matters: options on your man's next three fights, win or lose, at purses the champion's promoter sets. Sign it and the shot is real. Don't and the champion stays busy elsewhere — the rankings are patient and your fighter isn't.
choices: Sign the options (book the title fight)
Hold out for a purse bid / cleaner deal
Walk away from the shot
effects: Sign: title fight books at ×4 current purse scale. If he WINS: the next 3 defenses pay ×0.6 of open-market value (the option tax, itemized on each purse sheet) and the promoter picks the opponents; if he LOSES: options usually go quietly unexercised — the machine only wants winners. Fighter learns the terms: trust −5 now, +15 if he wins the belt anyway

Hold out: 6-12 month delay; 40% chance a cleaner shot materializes at ×3.5 (sanctioning politics from belt-inflation can force it); 35% chance the champion loses the belt or retires and the shot evaporates; fighter age ticks and if age ≥ 30, morale −10 during the wait
Walk: nothing now; glory_hunter morale −15 and a real quit-risk conversation; the ranking decays 2 places over the next year without marquee wins

triggeredEvents.title: The Sanctioning Fee
triggeredEvents.trigger: fighter first enters a body's national top-10 (fires per body once belt-inflation multiplies them)
triggeredEvents.story: A letter on heavy stationery: congratulations, your fighter is ranked #8. Enclosed, a schedule of 'ratings administration assessments' — due quarterly, in dollars, to a post-office box. Nothing in it says what happens if you don't pay. Nothing has to.
choices: Pay the assessment
Pay late and partial (haggle)
Refuse on principle
effects: Pay: $120 base-1975 per quarter (inflated) per body, a standing ledger line while ranked; ranking behaves normally
Haggle: pay 60%; ranking survives but 'slips' 1-2 places per year regardless of results — the invisible thumb

Refuse: 70% chance the fighter drops from that body's rankings within 2 quarters ('inactivity,' the letter says, though he fought twice); other bodies' rankings unaffected; one beat writer will print the story if the player's gym reputation is high enough — clipping runs, small reputation +, and that body's assessments quietly stop (they hate daylight)
triggeredEvents.frequency: common once ranked; recurring cost, one choice-event per body per fighter

triggeredEvents.title: An Arrangement
triggeredEvents.trigger: fighter age ≥ 29 + losses > wins + careerEarnings low for his age + a purse offer already on the table + gym cash < 3 months' overhead (it comes when you're weak)
triggeredEvents.story: A man you've seen at the weigh-ins — always at the edge of the photograph — catches you outside the gym. The purse for Tuesday could be four times bigger, he says, if your old-timer finds the canvas in the third and stays there. 'Nobody gets hurt. That's the whole point of it, friend. Nobody gets hurt.'
choices: Throw him out
Hear the number, then throw him out
Take the arrangement
effects: Throw him out: nothing visible. A ledger memory. Years later (if gym reputation ever crosses 'established'), an old beat writer's retrospective mentions the gym 'was never once mentioned in the wrong conversations' — permanent small reputation floor
Hear the number: same as above, but the fixer marks you as reachable — the event can fire again in a future squeeze, and the second offer is bigger

Take it: purse ×4. The fighter must be told: if lionheart or chip_on_shoulder or glory_hunter he REFUSES (trust craters −30, 50% he quits the gym and the story may surface). If he accepts (family_man + broke, or comfort_seeker, most likely): bout auto-resolves L/KO3, purse paid; his morale −20 and it never fully recovers (permanent baseline −5); 15% chance per subsequent year a commission investigator or writer resurfaces it — if it surfaces: license hearing, fine of the purse ×2 in that year's dollars, gym reputation −40%, every clean fighter with trust < 60 leaves
triggeredEvents.frequency: rare, at most twice per save

triggeredEvents.title: A Piece of the Gate
triggeredEvents.trigger: fighter publicReputation ≥ 60 + main-event offer at a casino or (post-ppv-arrives) PPV date
triggeredEvents.story: Two numbers on the contract, side by side. The guarantee, which is good. And the percentage, which is either half of that or three times it, depending on a snowstorm, the other guy's mouth, and whether the town shows up. The promoter slides it across like it's nothing. It is not nothing.
choices: Take the flat guarantee
Take the smaller guarantee plus percentage
effects: Flat: purse as offered, done

Percentage: guarantee ×0.5 up front; resolve multiplier from (combined publicReputation of both men /100) × era term × hype roll 0.6-1.8; final take ranges ×0.5 to ×4 of the flat number. A KO win in a percentage fight adds +4 extra publicReputation (the business notices a man who bets on himself and cashes); a dull decision in an empty house prints a brutal clipping

triggeredEvents.title: Promote It Yourself
triggeredEvents.trigger: fighter is a champion OR ranked top-3 + fighter homeCityId = gym city + gym reputation 'established' tier
triggeredEvents.story: The ballpark's general manager calls YOU for once. The champ defending at home, under the lights, twenty thousand seats — but nobody's putting up the money except the man in your mirror. Site rental, undercard, insurance, the sanctioning invoice. You'd be the promoter of record. Everything the last thirty years taught you says don't. Everything else says this is the whole point.
choices: Promote it (stake gym cash: $8,000 base-1975, inflated)
Sell the fight to a real promoter instead (safe purse)
Pass
effects: Promote: outcome = base gate × weather roll (0.7-1.15) × combined reputation term × win/loss of the bout itself. Range: lose a third of the stake to clearing ×3. A WIN at home: fighter morale +20, permanent trust +10, gym reputation jumps a tier step, a full-page clipping, and a framed fight bill appears in the office forever; a LOSS at home still sells tickets but the paper is unkind. Rain plus a loss is the worst financial night available in the game
Sell: standard title purse ×1.2 (hometown premium), no risk, no fight bill on the wall
Pass: glory_hunter or chip_on_shoulder fighter morale −10; the GM books a concert instead and the clipping mentions it
triggeredEvents.frequency: rare, once or twice per save

triggeredEvents.title: The Kid With the Notebook
triggeredEvents.trigger: gym has ≥ 2 fighters with bout records + gym reputation still small + year ≤ 1980 (he has to start young to grow old with you)
triggeredEvents.story: A matchmaker's assistant, maybe twenty-five, calls with a four-rounder that pays fair and matches honest. No angle you can find. When you take it and don't complain about the dressing room, he calls again the next month. Some men in this business you grow with.
choices: Take his fights when they're right (relationship builds passively)
Squeeze him on a purse once (test the relationship)
effects: Build: a hidden relationship counter rises each honest booking completed without a purse dispute. At counter ≥ 5: his offers arrive 20% above pool frequency and always 'fair' risk with accurate pitches. When cable-money fires, he surfaces as the weeknight-series matchmaker — your gym gets first call on the era's best working-fighter dates, worth years of steady purses. If a fighter of yours is ever stranded by a bounced-check event, he covers the date within 30 days
Squeeze: one-time +15% on that purse; counter resets to zero and caps at 3 forever ('he pays now, but he remembers'); the cable-era first-call never happens
triggeredEvents.frequency: once per save (the relationship itself is permanent)

triggeredEvents.title: The Purse That Wasn't There
triggeredEvents.trigger: purse ≥ $800 base-1975 (inflated) + promoter is small/unflagged OR the tournament-scandal 'crooked' NPC (20% chance on his offers)
triggeredEvents.story: The fight happened. The check didn't clear. The promoter's office phone rings eight times and then it doesn't ring at all — disconnected Thursday. Your fighter fought six hard rounds for a piece of paper.
choices: Eat it and pay the fighter's share from gym cash
Eat it together (fighter takes the loss too)
Lawyer and commission complaint
effects: Pay him yourself: gym cash −(fighter's 50% share); fighter trust +12 permanent ('he paid me out of his own pocket' — travels through the grapevine, all roster trust +3); the debt is memorialized in the ledger
Share the loss: fighter morale −15, trust −10; family_man or broke fighters −5 further; possible quit-risk if trust was already low

Lawyer: costs $150 base-1975 (inflated), 6-month process; 55% recovers the full purse plus the story printing as a clipping (gym reputation +small, 'a manager who collects'); 45% recovers nothing and the fee is gone

triggeredEvents.title: Selling Your Own Tickets
triggeredEvents.trigger: fighter record ≤ 4 fights + club-show offer in home city + pre-club-show-collapse era (this is how it actually worked)
triggeredEvents.story: The club promoter's terms come with a rubber band around them: fifty tickets at four dollars. Your kid fights if the tickets move. 'He's got a neighborhood, don't he?' the promoter says. Every four-round fighter in America is also a ticket salesman, and now so are you.
choices: Take the tickets and hustle them (fighter sells)
Buy the allotment yourself
Refuse the terms
effects: Hustle: success scales with fighter's publicReputation + chip_on_shoulder/family_man bonus (neighborhood roots) — full sale nets the purse plus $40 walking-around money and morale +6 ('the whole block was there'); a failed sale (reputation < 8, insecure trait) cuts the purse 40% and morale −8
Buy them: gym cash −$200 base-1975 (inflated), purse intact, fight proceeds; a quiet trust +4 (he knows)
Refuse: offer lost; club promoters in the city tag the gym 'difficult' for 6 months (−15% novice offer frequency)
triggeredEvents.frequency: common in the first era, once per fighter's early career; extinct after club-show-collapse completes

triggeredEvents.title: Ten Days' Notice
triggeredEvents.trigger: a TV-era active + fighter not booked + restUntil passed + record ≥ 10 fights + morale ≥ 40 (they call men who are in the gym)
triggeredEvents.story: The phone at 11 p.m., which is never good news or is the best news: the co-feature fell out, the date is in ten days, and the purse is double because everyone else already said no. The opponent is better than anything your man has seen. That's why the purse is double.
choices: Take it
Take it, but negotiate a no-cut clause (purse ×1.7 instead of ×2)
Let it go
effects: Take: bout books in 10 days at ×2 purse against a 'reach'-window opponent; conditionOf capped at 0.78 (no camp); a WIN here is the single biggest reputation event below a title (+16, 'the kid who said yes') and TV matchmakers flag him 'reliable' (+1 TV offer frequency permanently); a bad KO loss on short notice: normal damage +ring-tragedy-era scrutiny if active
No-cut: same but a stoppage-on-cuts converts to a technical draw (protects the record at a price)
Pass: no penalty — but if the fighter is reckless_brave or glory_hunter and hears about it (50%): morale −8 and one gym-log line of him hitting the bag after hours

triggeredEvents.title: The Casino Wants Him Steady
triggeredEvents.trigger: desert-money era + fighter wins ≥ 12 + publicReputation 40-65 + crowd-pleasing profile (kos/wins ≥ 0.5 OR showman/pressure style)
triggeredEvents.story: The casino's entertainment director offers a retainer: four fights a year on their cards, guaranteed money, his face on the little easel by the sports book. The catch is in the passive voice: opponents 'will be arranged.' Your man becomes furniture — well-paid, well-lit furniture.
choices: Sign the retainer (2 years)
Decline and stay independent
effects: Sign: 4 guaranteed bouts/year at ×1.8 club scale each, paid even if a date scratches; opponents chosen by the house — mostly 'soft,' occasionally a 'reach' when they need him to lose to a rising name (1 in 6, unannounced); publicReputation gains capped at +3 per win (beating arranged men impresses nobody); comfort_seeker fighter: morale +10 and training effort sags; glory_hunter: morale −6 per soft bout, will eventually demand out (trust −10 if refused)
Decline: normal offer flow continues; the entertainment director shrugs — no freeze-out, casinos are businesslike about no

triggeredEvents.title: He Found Out What the Other Guy Made
triggeredEvents.trigger: post-fight + fighter's purse < opponent's known purse × 0.5 + fighter has insecure OR chip_on_shoulder trait
triggeredEvents.story: Somebody at the weigh-in talked, the way somebody always does. Your man fought the same eight rounds in the same ring and made a third of the money, and he's been doing arithmetic on the bus home ever since.
choices: Level with him — show him the books and the plan
Give him a bonus from the gym's share
Tell him that's the business
effects: Level: trust check — if trust ≥ 55, he accepts it (trust +5, morale −3, 'at least he's straight with me'); if trust < 55, morale −10 and the doubt lingers (small recurring morale drag for 3 months)
Bonus: gym cash −20% of the purse; morale +8; but a precedent counter starts — every future underpaid fight expects it, and skipping one later costs double the trust
The business: chip_on_shoulder channels it (training effort +10% for 2 months, morale −5); insecure spirals (morale −15, trust −8, quit-risk if morale < 30)

triggeredEvents.title: The Medalist Comes to Town
triggeredEvents.trigger: Olympic-summer years (1976, 1980, 1984, 1988, 1992...) + gym reputation ≥ regional tier + gym cash ≥ $1,000 base-1975 (inflated)
triggeredEvents.story: The Games end and the amateurs turn over. One of them — a medal, a smile the cameras liked — is touring gyms with his father and a lawyer. Every promoter in the country has already mailed the family something. Yours is the smallest operation on the list, which is either an insult or the only honest option he's got.
choices: Bid for him: signing money ($1,500 base-1975, inflated) + a locker + a focused-training slot promised
Court him cheap: no money, just the pitch (gym's development record does the talking)
Stay out of it
effects: Bid: 35% he signs (higher if gym has produced a ranked fighter — the record is the pitch); arrives as a generated fighter with quality ≥ 0.75, publicReputation 25 (a known amateur), and a hidden trait rolled normally — medals don't tell you who a man is; if outbid, money returned but the clipping notes your gym 'was in the conversation' (+small reputation)
Court: 10% base, but 40% if any current roster fighter is ranked AND trusts you ≥ 70 (the kid calls him and asks what you're really like — the roster is the recruiter)
Out: nothing; he signs with a promoter's stable and becomes a world-sim name you read about for a decade
triggeredEvents.frequency: every Olympic cycle, one kid per cycle

triggeredEvents.title: The Doctor Doesn't Like What He Sees
triggeredEvents.trigger: post-ring-tragedy-reform era + fighter age ≥ 31 + career KO losses ≥ 3 + a bout booked (the new medicals catch him at the pre-fight)
triggeredEvents.story: The commission physician holds your fighter's license paperwork a beat too long. The new rules give him the pen: 'irregularities' — he wants a specialist's clearance before the man fights again in this state. The specialist is in another city, costs real money, and might say no.
choices: Pay for the specialist workup ($200 base-1975, inflated)
Fight him in a looser state instead (venue changes, purse −25%)
Read the handwriting: retire him
effects: Specialist: 70% cleared (bout proceeds, paper trail protects you forever after); 30% not cleared — license suspended in-state, and now you KNOW, and everything you book for him after is a choice you made with knowledge (if he later takes serious damage anywhere, gym reputation −30% when the story runs, and it runs)

Looser state: bout proceeds at reduced purse; the beat writer notices the venue change and files it away; can be done twice before a column runs ('Why Won't Any Doctor Here Look at Him?') — reputation −10

Retire him: purse lost, roster spot opens; trust of ALL roster fighters +6 ('he wouldn't feed a hurt man to the wolves'); the fighter himself — family_man goes gratefully (leaves as a friend, may return as a coach applicant in 2-3 years); glory_hunter or lionheart fights it bitterly (morale collapse, may quit and get licensed elsewhere as a world-sim independent, which you will read about with your stomach in your shoes)
triggeredEvents.frequency: uncommon in the reform era, once per at-risk fighter

hills: MONEY ALWAYS COSTS CONTROL. The option-contract / buyout / house-retainer lattice (options-for-the-shot, contract-buyout, house-fighter-retainer, casino-b-side) must ship as a connected system, not four flavor pop-ups: every purse above club scale carries a string the player can read, price, and refuse — and refusal has a real, quiet cost (freeze-outs, delays, decayed rankings). This is the actual texture of the boxing business in these decades, and it's what makes the money screen a strategy screen instead of a slot machine. Cut anything else before you cut the strings.

THE ACCOMMODATION STAYS IN, WITH TEETH BOTH WAYS. The fixer's dive offer is the genre's defining values choice, and it only works if (a) it arrives when the player is genuinely broke, (b) the fighter's TRAITS decide whether he'll even do it — a lionheart refuses and it costs you HIM, and (c) the consequence is a years-later fuse, not an instant fine. No morality meter, no red warning text — just a man outside the gym and a ledger you have to live with. If the Lead sands this down to a safe 'reject scam' popup, we've lost the one event people will tell each other about.

THE VENUE ECONOMY MUST DIE AND BE REBORN UNDER THE PLAYER'S FEET. Club-show-collapse plus desert-money plus cable-money is one arc: where fights happen and what they pay has to actually change across a 20-year save — a persistent local venue really closes, novice offers really thin, the cable series really replaces them — or the decades are just 1975 with 6% bigger numbers. This is cheap to implement (venue list edits, frequency terms, purse multipliers already in pursefor's shape) and it's the single strongest proof the world is alive.
